Windows `ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE`, **17 occurrences**; socket churn refuted at 0.104.0; occurrence 8 (local) argues local ≠ CI, and occurrence 9 landed on a DOCS-ONLY PR, and occurrence 10's same-run A/B shows the PASSING shard MORE loaded on peak TIME_WAIT, handles, processes and non-paged pool — the countable axis is refuted for both symptom classes; see R4.58. **Occurrence 11 (0.115.0, run 32547205251, `test_flows.py::test_mutate_flow_is_approval_gated_by_default` at `Page.goto`) INDEPENDENTLY REPLICATES that A/B on an unrelated PR**: failing shard 1 vs passing shard 2 — TIME_WAIT max 331 vs 361, handles 53112 vs 54894, non-paged pool 225.7 vs 240.5 MB, paged pool 327.3 vs 368.0, processes 154 vs 153. Every countable axis LOWER on the arm that died, with 206 ephemeral TIME_WAIT against 16384 available ports, so exhaustion is not close. The ONE column that points the other way is `chrome_procs` (max 8 vs 5), which is the concurrent-Chromium hypothesis `ci.yml` already names — recorded at its true weight, which with a single pair is an observation and not evidence. The 5 s sampling interval also makes every max a FLOOR on the true peak, so a sub-5 s spike is invisible to this instrument in both arms. **Occurrence 12** (0.118.0, run 32604870523, `test_trust_state.py::test_dry_run_names_a_migration_stale_approval` at `Page.goto`) adds no new analysis and is recorded for the COUNT, which is what this entry tracks and which CI logs do not keep. Windows shard 2 again; green on a same-commit re-run, with `src/` unchanged since the run where that test passed **Occurrence 13** (0.119.0, LOCAL — the second one on a developer host, after occurrence 8) is the first with a SECOND-ORDER effect worth recording. It killed `drift_bench`'s shared `_record()` fixture at `Page.goto`, so the 13 `test_drift_bench.py` cells that depend on it never launched a browser — and the run was a `--store-browser-marks` run, which therefore DE-CLASSIFIED all 13 into the fast tier. A flake in the browser is thus a silent corruption of the tier manifest, where the failure mode is not a red test but 13 browser tests being deselected from the fast tier forever. The two-phase regeneration caught it exactly as designed: the fixed-point loop re-ran the fast tier, all 13 launched, all 13 were promoted back, converged in one round, and the committed delta is +17 fast / 0 browser. Recorded because it prices the manifest's second phase — the loop is not a tidy-up for order-dependence, it is the only thing standing between a flaky browser and a manifest that quietly stops running a module. **Occurrence 14** (0.141.0, run 33139153836, PR #221, `test_drift_bench.py::test_every_absolute_invariant_holds` at `Page.goto` on a local fixture URL) is recorded for the COUNT, which is what this entry tracks. Two details worth the line. **It is windows shard 1**, where occurrences 11-13 were all shard 2 -- so the shard is not a stable signature and any hypothesis keyed on shard 2 specifically is refuted by this row. And the PR that carried it **touches no `src/` at all**: it adds twelve browser-free cells and documentation, which is occurrence 9's docs-only argument repeated on a second commit -- the failure cannot be caused by what the PR changes. Green on a same-commit re-run of the failed job. Nothing here narrows the cause; the honest content is the count, the shard, and that the change surface was again empty. **Occurrence 15** (0.143.0, run 33225811103, PR #223, windows shard **2/2**, `test_miniwob.py::test_miniwob_click_button_learn_then_replay` at `Page.goto` on a local fixture url) is the FIRST with a within-shard RESOURCE TIME SERIES at the failure instant, and it buys one real negative plus one more refutation. **THE NEGATIVE: ephemeral-port exhaustion is refuted AT THE MOMENT, not by peak comparison.** The windows dynamic range is 16384 ports from 49152, and `time_wait` at the failing sample was **126** -- 0.8% utilisation. Its peak of 366 came at elapsed 386 s, twelve minutes BEFORE the failure at ~1116 s, so the symptom does not even correlate with the axis its own name (`ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE` = `WSAENOBUFS`) invites. **THE REFUTATION: a non-paged pool lead looked strong and died on rate normalisation.** Within the failing shard the non-paged pool climbs MONOTONICALLY 165.4 -> 243.3 MB (non-decreasing in 110 of 154 samples) and the failure fires exactly at its maximum, which is the shape a pool leak would have. But the same-run A/B this register already runs kills it: the failing shard ran **25% longer** (1117 s vs 896 s) and is only 1-3% higher on every axis, and per second the PASSING shard leaked FASTER -- **0.081 MB/s vs 0.070 MB/s** non-paged growth. 'At its maximum when it failed' is a property of any monotonically-growing series sampled at the end of a long run, not a discriminator. That is the THIRD consecutive same-run A/B to point the wrong way (occurrences 10, 11, 15) and it applies to the same axes each time. **AND THE CHANGE SURFACE WAS AGAIN EMPTY**: PR #223 touches no `src/` -- docs, a benchmark probe and its tests -- which is the third such PR to carry this (occurrences 9, 14, 15), so the failure cannot be caused by what the PR changes. Shard 2/2 here where 14 was shard 1, which is the shard signature staying refuted. Green on a same-commit re-run. **WHAT THE SERIES IS WORTH KEEPING FOR**: it is the first artifact that can answer 'what did the machine look like at the failure' rather than 'after cleanup', and the post-job telemetry block reads 118 TIME_WAIT because it samples after the run ends -- anyone reading that number as the failure condition is reading a drained pool. **Occurrence 16** (0.145.0, run 33261967361, PR #225, windows shard **1/2**, `test_drift_bench.py::test_every_absolute_invariant_holds` at `Page.goto` on `127.0.0.1:50837/ladder`) is the SAME TEST as occurrence 14 and the FOURTH same-run A/B, and it buys the first CROSS-OCCURRENCE comparison because two at-failure time series now exist. **THE A/B POINTS THE WRONG WAY AGAIN, and more cleanly than ever**: the PASSING shard peaked higher on FOUR of five axes -- non-paged pool 236.4 vs 228.6, paged 353.3 vs 347.2, TIME_WAIT 373 vs 337, handles 55954 vs 53629 -- with only `processes` higher on the failing side (156 vs 155, noise). **AND DURATION IS KILLED AS THE CONFOUND IT WAS IN OCCURRENCE 15**: there the failing shard ran 25% LONGER, which is what explained its higher peaks; here the failing shard ran SHORTER (955 s vs 1140 s) and still failed. So neither absolute load nor run length discriminates. **NO COMMON AT-FAILURE SIGNATURE EXISTS ACROSS THE TWO INCIDENTS**, which is the new negative and the reason this occurrence was worth measuring: at the failing sample, occurrence 15 read non-paged 243.3 MB with TIME_WAIT 126, and occurrence 16 reads non-paged 227.8 MB with TIME_WAIT **216** -- the port count nearly doubled while the pool fell 15 MB. No threshold on any measured axis is consistent with both, so a 'resource crosses a line' theory is refuted on the only two incidents where the line could be checked. Rate normalisation does not rescue it either: occurrence 16's failing shard grew the pool at 0.0623 MB/s against the passing shard's 0.0574, the OPPOSITE ordering to occurrence 15 (0.0697 failing vs 0.0805 passing). **The change surface was again empty** -- PR #225 touches no `src/` -- which is the fourth such PR (9, 14, 15, 16). Green on a re-run. **Occurrence 17** (0.150.0, LOCAL, `Page.goto: net::ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE` at a drift_bench fixture url) is only the SECOND local one and the first with a deliberate trigger: a harness running `drift_bench.measure` **four times back to back in ONE process** died partway through the first run. Every CI occurrence is a single suite pass; this is repeated benches in one interpreter, and it failed on a host measured minutes earlier at 2 chromium/node processes, 11.5 GB free of 32 GB and idle containers -- so it is not ambient load. **That is a REPRODUCTION LEVER this entry has never had**, and worth trying deliberately before the next theory: 16 occurrences have produced no cause because each was one sample nobody could re-run. Recorded rather than pursued -- the A/B it interrupted was about something else -- but anyone returning to R4.22 should start here. **Occurrence 18** (0.160.0, run 33585872596 job 100109782038, PR #240, windows shard **1/2**, `test_drift_bench.py::test_every_absolute_invariant_holds` at `Page.goto` on the local fixture `127.0.0.1:59030/order-form`; 1 failed / 1223 passed in 18m55s) is recorded for the COUNT, which is what this entry tracks and CI logs do not keep. **The change surface was again EMPTY** -- PR #240 touches no `src/` at all (docs, a register correction, one test file and one benchmark probe) -- which is the FIFTH such PR (occurrences 9, 14, 15, 16, 18), so the failure cannot be caused by what the PR changes. **And it is the THIRD occurrence on this same test**, after 14 and 16, all three on windows shard 1. That concentration is NOT offered as a lead: `test_every_absolute_invariant_holds` drives the whole drift bench and therefore issues far more `Page.goto` calls than any other cell, so it has the largest exposure by construction and would top a purely random distribution too. Weighting by goto count before reading anything into it is the arithmetic nobody has done. Occurrence 15 (shard 2) already refuted the shard signature and still does.

the wire promotion marks ordinary GraphQL-style READS as writes (12/12 measured) **SURVEYED 2026-08-27 (0.140.0) — `docs/reads-over-post.md`.** Eleven approaches, each with an adversarial pass. **SIX ARE DEAD**, three of them killed by that pass rather than by prior history: two-tier marking (C) reaches 0/10 because the measured refusals are GATE refusals, which return pre-act, and the heal paths are themselves `is_write_request` consumers so recovery stays poisoned after restoration; the navigate-gate (G) is vacuous on Odoo, where every backend page is origin+path `/web` with all state in the hash it would have to tolerate; response evidence (E) is measured barren (200 for reads, writes AND errors, identical headers) and actively wrong because `web_save` returns the saved record read back. Operator declaration (D) and frequency (F) die on their failure DIRECTION. **THE LEAD IS A JSON-RPC READ-METHOD ALLOWLIST plus a route-EXACT read-route list**, failing closed on everything else: it is the only approach reaching the measured population (10/10), the request body is a sensor class D5 has not spent, and the recorded denylist refusal does not transfer — that refusal reads "a GraphQL MUTATION travels the same URL", whereas an Odoo `create` cannot travel under the name `search_read` because the method name IS the operation (`getattr(model, method)` dispatch). Prior art is unanimous that nobody classifies POST-tunneled reads by method. **NOT SCHEDULED, AND ONE ASSUMPTION IS UNPRICED**: that fixing the marking improves Odoo availability at all. R4.111's tail is the counter-signal — one gate refusal was itself `target missing/ambiguous`, and the READ path also resolves `unique=True`, so demotion may only convert "gate refused" into "healed and still failed". Six free measurements settle it, listed in the doc; #1 (flip the cached marks and replay) decides whether the whole ranking holds. **THE JSON-RPC HALF IS FIXED AT 0.150.0 (R4.123, D7's approach B): `safety.body_says_read` clears an Odoo-style `call_kw` POST whose body names a read, so those steps stop being gated. THE GRAPHQL HALF -- this finding's ORIGINAL 12/12 population -- IS UNTOUCHED**, because reads and mutations share one endpoint there and the operation lives in a query string the rule does not parse. That is approach A in `docs/reads-over-post.md`, unbuilt, and `test_annotation_disposition.py` still pins the GraphQL controls caching as write flows.

`_learn` snapshots straight after navigate with no settle floor, so a client-rendered page is authored against its unrendered skeleton — quiet, and one variant PERSISTS a refusal **AND THE REPLAY TWIN IS R4.115 (0.142.0), WHICH IS THE FATAL HALF.** The same missing settle floor is on the replay path, where it is not quiet: the locator resolve, the gate's scope fingerprint and the gate's whole-page snapshot all read an unpainted page and report DRIFT. Note which way the guard went -- this finding's mitigation (`assert_not_a_skeleton`, `SKELETON_ELEMENT_FLOOR`, measured at 5 by R4.93) lives in `benchmarks/substrates.py` and guards the LEARN's start page only. Nothing guards the replay anywhere, in `src/` or in the bench. That is CLAUDE.md's named predictor -- a guard on a sibling path never applied to the mechanism -- and it is also why the learn survives at all: the author loop RE-OBSERVES every turn, while the replay resolves once and has its heal provider nulled. **AND R4.118 (0.143.0) IS WHAT IT COSTS, MEASURED ON THE PRODUCT RATHER THAN THE HARNESS.** Five bought Odoo learns: one healthy recipe, two that are 100% `navigate` steps (20 of 20 and 8 of 8, one re-navigating to the same url 12 times), two that cached nothing after 21 actions. An agent that cannot see whether the page arrived re-navigates, and the resulting recipe caches as a SUCCESS. This finding's mitigation guards the learn's START page from `benchmarks/`; nothing guards the steps the learn then authors, in the bench or in `src/`. **FIXED AT 0.146.0 -- THE LEARN SETTLES BEFORE IT LOOKS.** `BrowserSession.await_settled()` resolves once the DOM has been free of mutations for `settle_quiet_ms` (200, MEASURED by R4.120 as the cheapest predicate that is never premature over 60 page-reps), capped at `settle_cap_ms` (2000). Every mutation RESTARTS the quiet timer, so it is 'the page stopped changing' and not 'some time passed' -- R4.26's rule, honoured by taking the fact from the platform. `_author_steps` calls it at BOTH observation sites: before the loop-head snapshot, so the agent decides from the page rather than its skeleton, and before the verify snapshot, which is the half that re-arms the bail. **MEASURED ON REAL ODOO, before and after, six navigations to the SAME url**: without the settle the observation is 5-6 elements and `no_progress` ends at **0** (it reaches 3 and then RESETS when a stray fingerprint change reads as progress, which is exactly how a learn burns its budget); with it the observation is **80 elements every time** and `no_progress` climbs cleanly to **4**, the `stuck_limit`. Every settle returned `quiet`, never `cap`. **FAIL-OPEN BY CONSTRUCTION**: a page mid-navigation makes `evaluate` throw and the settle returns `unavailable`; on the cap it gives up and the caller proceeds. Both are exactly the behaviour before this existed, so the worst case of the mechanism is 'no better than before', never 'worse'. `drift_bench` re-run because this adds a MutationObserver that runs IN THE PAGE: **invariants ALL HOLD**, `silent_wrong` 2 (the published allowlist row), writes double=0 suppressed=0 wrong_target=0, recovery refused on 14/14 drifted write rows. **THE REPLAY HALF IS NOT THIS FINDING AND STAYS OPEN AS R4.115**, deliberately: its cost profile is the opposite (a server-rendered page measures `true_ready = 0` in every rep, so an unconditional wait there is pure tax on the speed claim), so it needs the CONDITIONAL two-state sensor rather than this. `test_replay_is_deliberately_untouched` pins that the call sites number exactly two, both on the learn path.

a fixture sub-resource silently fails to load and surfaces as a JS `ReferenceError`; the HTTP/1.0 socket-churn cause is REFUTED by measurement (8 vs 6 connections per load) and a sweep would risk 8 hangs — disposition is the shared fixture server **OCCURRENCE 2 (0.123.0, PR #202, run 32680159360, windows shard 2/2).** `test_miniwob_click_button_learn_then_replay` failed with `TypeError: Math.seedrandom is not a function`. Diagnosed rather than assumed: MiniWoB's task page is served by a LOCAL static fixture server and pulls three sub-resources; `Math.seedrandom` is defined by the minified seedrandom library embedded inside `core/core.js`, which assigns `b["seed"+o]=c` — so a literal `Math.seedrandom =` grep finds nothing and the definition is easy to mistake for an external dependency. No CDN is involved. `core.js` therefore failed to load from the fixture server and the page reported it in JS terms rather than as a connection error, which is this finding's shape exactly. INTERMITTENT: the same job passed on re-run with no change, so it cost one 17-minute CI job and NOT a slice — the trigger for un-holding 0.7 is a shape occurrence that COSTS A SLICE, and by that wording it has still not fired. Recorded because the next one now has a precedent, and because the count is the thing CI logs do not keep. Note also what this occurrence is NOT: ubuntu passed both shards and the failure is windows-only, which is R4.22's platform signature without R4.22's symptom — the two may share a socket-pressure cause and nothing here establishes that. **OCCURRENCE 3 (0.124.0, PR #203, run 32694571491, windows shard 2/2 again).** `test_recorder_cracks_the_garbled_label_ceiling_0llm` failed with `ReferenceError: ui_utils is not defined`. Same diagnosis, verified the same way: `ui_utils` is defined by `miniwob/html/common/ui_utils.js`, a sub-resource of the LOCAL fixture server, so the symbol being undefined means that file did not load. A DIFFERENT sub-resource from occurrence 2 (`core/core.js`), a different test, the same shape — a fixture file failing to load locally and surfacing as a JavaScript error naming a symbol the missing file defines, which is why these read as product bugs until someone traces the symbol. INTERMITTENT again: all nine checks green on re-run with no change. **WHAT HAS CHANGED IS THE RATE, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF RECORDING IT.** Three occurrences, the last two in CONSECUTIVE slices, all three on windows shard 2/2, each costing a ~19-minute CI job. The trigger for un-holding 0.7 (the shared fixture server) is a shape occurrence that COSTS A SLICE, and by that wording it has STILL not fired — two re-runs is not a slice, and un-holding a plan step on a rate rather than on its stated trigger is the ad-hoc picking `correctness-plan.md` exists to prevent. But whoever next reads 0.7's hold should read this count with it, because CI logs expire and the count is what they do not keep. The windows-only signature is now three for three, which is R4.22's platform signature without R4.22's symptom; that they share a socket-pressure cause remains a HYPOTHESIS and nothing here tests it.
findings.disposition: reshape-plan step 0.7 (shared fixture server) — explicitly NOT a protocol sweep

findings.summary: a SUCCESSFUL run reports the failed attempt's `failure_code` — `_attempt_replay`'s success exit sets `ok` but never clears it, and `_mark_ok` (which does) is only called on the precheck and relearn exits; found by the exit-set matrix on its first run — FIXED at 0.110.0 by THE SINK (reshape-plan 1.5): `ok` and `failure_code` are decided once, from whether `replay()` raised, so a successful run cannot inherit the code of an attempt that failed on the way
findings.disposition: reshape-plan step 1.5, landed

findings.summary: the R4.22 resource sampler measures the wrong quantity: a Windows shard failed TWICE on two DIFFERENT browser tests, both latency-shaped (a 5s Locator.wait_for timeout; a write confirm missing inside its budget), while the same run's PASSING Windows shard was the MORE loaded of the two on 4 of 7 sampled metrics — the first same-run healthy baseline, and it refutes resource exhaustion for this symptom class. Neither CPU nor disk I/O is sampled, which is what a latency failure is about
findings.disposition: add CPU and disk-queue sampling before the next occurrence is diagnosed; do NOT re-derive the socket/handle hypotheses, which this measurement rules out for timeouts

findings.summary: a strict xfail added by 0.3 ASSERTED the counterexample — it demanded that `replay()` overwrite an UNKNOWN cost with a confident zero, the understated bill B1 exists to prevent, and `strict=True` made it a standing demand that 1.5 implement it. R4.51 was a coverage gap, not a behaviour defect: the two cases already differ. FIXED by rewriting the cell as the distinguishability property it was named for; src untouched
findings.disposition: closed at 1.5's first step; the two coercion mutants are registered so red-proof keeps them dead

findings.summary: `scripts/prove_red.py` scores a PERFECT run when its killer suite collects nothing: a mutant is judged killed by a non-zero pytest exit, so a `--tests` path that does not collect makes every mutant 'killed'. An audit hit it and read 17/17 where the honest number was 16/17. The same failure shape the script already guards on the other side (a stale find-text is an ERROR, not a survivor), one step over — an instrument reporting the suite as stronger than it is. FIXED at 0.110.0: the killer suite must collect and pass on the UNMUTATED tree before any mutation is applied
findings.disposition: closed at 1.5's audit round; armed by pointing --tests at a path that does not exist

findings.summary: `write_unverified` records `committed=False` while its own message says the commit ACTUATED — `_fail` appends `outcome="failed"`, which is not in `_UNKNOWN_OUTCOMES`, so the fold answers the write question 'no' for the one kind whose whole meaning is 'it fired and cannot be confirmed'. NOT a regression (the pre-sink code did the same), but the sink's stated rule was supposed to close this class and does not, because unanswerability is keyed on the outcome STRING and every failure exit shares one. The human channel is covered (the exception text says to check the target system); the record is not — FIXED at 0.112.0 (reshape-plan 1.4b): `_evidence` keys on the FIELD rather than the outcome STRING, `_UNKNOWN_OUTCOMES` is deleted, and `_AttemptFacts` defaults both write fields to None so an append site that states nothing is UNKNOWN rather than a denial. `write_unverified` records `committed=None`; the two ARMING tokens keep their conservative False
findings.disposition: reshape-plan step 1.4b, landed

findings.summary: `playwright install` exits 0 when the host is missing a Chromium shared library. Verified in the installed driver: `coreBundle.js:64433` ends the CLI install with `validateHostRequirementsForExecutablesIfNeeded(...).catch(e => { e.name = 'Playwright Host validation warning'; console.error(e) })` — the ldd verdict is renamed to a warning and discarded. NOT silent overall: the same call at `coreBundle.js:38335`, on the LAUNCH path, is awaited with no catch and throws, so the first browser test fails loudly. The cost is ATTRIBUTION, which is this slice's own class one door over — a provisioning fault presents as a test failure, ~1 min into the suite instead of at a step called `Install Chromium`. It became load-bearing at reshape-plan step 0, when `--with-deps` was dropped and the runner image became the thing supplying those libraries
findings.disposition: A smoke-launch step after the install was DESIGNED and REFUSED in the step-0 slice, for a reason that still holds: a hand-rolled launcher is a second transcription of `src/ultracua/browser.py`'s launch path, and headless resolves to `chromium_headless_shell`, a DIFFERENT binary from the `chromium` the suite may exec — so it could certify the wrong one and be green while the real path fails. If taken, it must go through `ultracua.browser`'s own launch rather than re-deriving it, must run on Linux only (windows has never had this failure mode and carries R4.22's launch-churn suspect), and must be pinned against being rewritten to a no-op — S14's three inert cells are the precedent

findings.summary: The shard count is TRANSCRIBED three times and reconciled nowhere: `scripts/check_shard_coverage.py`'s `SPLITS = 2`, `ci.yml`'s `group: [1, 2]`, and `ci.yml`'s `--splits 2`. Moving to three shards in the workflow leaves `check_shard_coverage` silently asserting a 2-way partition — it would keep passing while the property it exists to prove (union == full collection, no duplicates) went unchecked for the real partition. Same shape as `flow_key_transcriptions` and the other ratcheted transcription classes, and the instrument that closes it now exists
findings.disposition: `tests/test_ci_provisioning.py` (step 0) already parses ci.yml totally; deriving SPLITS from the workflow rather than declaring it is a few lines on top of that parser. NOT taken in step 0 to keep the slice to one thing, and because adding cells costs a ~55 min tier-manifest re-derivation that reshape-plan step 0.8 is about to make free

findings.summary: In `fast`, `red-proof` and `shard-coverage`, network provisioning and the work are FUSED into a single `- run:` — `uv run --group bench --group providers --group mcp pytest -q --tier fast` resolves and downloads from PyPI before pytest starts. Step 0’s step budgets therefore name nothing in those three jobs: 'the fast tier step timed out' still cannot say whether the index hung or the tier hung, which is verbatim the defect step 0 exists to close, surviving in the three jobs it did not reach. The `test` job has the same shape one level down — its first `uv run` is the `Install Chromium` step, which silently carries the whole sync
findings.disposition: Split each fused step into a budgeted `uv sync` and a budgeted work step, so a provisioning over-run names itself in every job rather than only in `test`. Deliberately deferred from step 0: the measured fault was on the `test` job's ubuntu arm and the fix there was a REMOVAL, whereas this is a restructuring of three healthy jobs with no observed failure behind it — worth doing, not worth bundling. Note `setup-uv`'s `enable-cache: true` means a cold cache is the unmeasured case; the budgets chosen in step 0 assume a warm one

findings.summary: `scripts/manifest_cost.py`'s executable rule silently flipped to recommending the design CLAUDE.md refuses. Clause (b) -- 'the thing merging would lose is not happening' -- read a ROLLING WINDOW (`deltas[1:][-10:]`), so once the sole de-classifying revision (35357b5, three tests, the fast tier's own arming cells) scrolled past ten, `report` began printing 'VERDICT: SWITCH to merge-mode' on every invocation. `docs/reshape-plan.md` §13 had stated 24 hours earlier that clause (b) refuses merge-mode 'permanently as far as the data goes'; nothing about the workflow had changed, the window had moved. De-classification is a CAPABILITY, not a recent-events statistic: one observation proves merging would freeze a real event and a quiet stretch does not unprove it. Note `tests/test_manifest_cost.py:166` already asserted the honest form (`any(d.declassified for d in deltas[1:])`) and stayed green throughout -- the rule and its own test were reading different histories. FIXED: clause (b) reads all of history; `test_an_OLD_declassification_still_refuses_the_merge` arms an old event plus a 40-delta clean tail, verified RED against the rolling-window rule

The tier manifest's write path was guarded on ONE axis of four, and two of the open ones destroy it silently while printing success. `write_manifest()` classifies from `PER_TEST` (what RAN) while `guard_full_collection` checked `COLLECTED` (what was collected). (i) SHARDING: pytest-split deselects AFTER the root conftest records COLLECTED, so under `--splits 2 --group 1` COLLECTED is 1201 while only 626 run -- the guard passes and the write would delete ~575 classifications. This is what CI runs on every PR, and it is the axis any CI-derived-marks design must emit from. (ii) COLLECT-ONLY: measured live, `pytest -q --collect-only --store-browser-marks` printed 'wrote .browser_tests.json: 0 browser, 0 fast' over 1201 classifications and reported success. `PartialDerivation`'s own docstring says the `--tier` guard 'covered the wrong axis'; there were two more. FIXED with two sensors rather than two more flag checks: `guard_not_narrowed` (selected < collected -- catches --splits/-k/-m/--deselect together) and `guard_every_selected_test_ran` (REPORTS, not PER_TEST, because a SKIPPED test never runs the autouse probe and keying on PER_TEST would refuse any machine that legitimately skips -- measured 3 items / 2 skipped / 3 reported / 1 in PER_TEST)
findings.disposition: Found while scouting reshape-plan step 0.8 (CI-derived marks), which cannot be built on a write path that silently truncates from a sharded observation. Shipped ahead of 0.8 as its prerequisite

findings.summary: The tier manifest could only be re-derived by a full local suite run -- twelve ledger entries at 1917-3151 s -- while CI already ran that same suite four times per PR (two shards x two OSes) and threw the launch evidence away. Three consecutive slices paid ~36 min each to add six, four and three browser-free cells. FIXED at step 0.8: `pytest --emit-marks PATH` writes an OBSERVATION (collected/selected/reported/launches) and never the manifest, so a shard may emit evidence although it may never write a classification; `scripts/tier_marks.py merge` checks a contract and writes a CANDIDATE, validates THAT with the fixed-point loop via ULTRACUA_TIER_MANIFEST, and swaps only on convergence. Local-first by correction: an earlier design made CI the sole supplier, which needed an open PR + gh auth + no concurrent push + a 16-25 min wait with the 36-min local run as fallback -- moving the tax behind a network precondition rather than removing it

Identity for a set of tier marks is the COLLECTED ID SET, never a commit sha, and a sha-keyed design would have been silently wrong. On a `pull_request` GitHub checks out `refs/pull/N/merge`, not the branch tip: run 32380417760 reports headSha 5d47964 while its checkout log says `HEAD is now at 2c908fc Merge 5d47964 into 4f7ac67`. So a run correctly IDENTIFIED by a commit collected a DIFFERENT tree, and once main has moved that tree carries tests the developer does not have. The resulting inflated `total` would then DISARM the deletion detector in `tests/test_tiers.py`, which only runs when `len(collected) >= data['total']` -- the fault switching off its own alarm. Refusing on the id set also covers a stale part, a part from main, and a tree edited after the push, with no extra sensors and no clean-tree check. Demonstrated live during the slice: a test renamed after the observation was emitted was refused in 2 s, naming both sides of the difference

The H9 quarantine's READ twin eats the value-contract reason, and a test docstring asserts the mitigation that does not exist. `_quarantine` wraps its `_update_meta` in `except MetaUnwritableError` and re-raises carrying the H9 reason (R4.17) — the READ half, `MetaUnreadableError`, is not caught, so it escapes `_do_quarantine` bare and the operator is told about a sidecar IO error instead of about a wrong VALUE. Reproduced with a control: armed, the escaping message carries no trace of the finding; unarmed, the quarantine persists. `tests/test_meta_load_provenance.py::test_an_unreadable_sidecar_does_not_replace_the_H9_quarantine_reason` states in its docstring that "`_do_quarantine` catches it and still raises `FlowQuarantineError` with the H9 reason plus a note that persistence failed" — `_do_quarantine` (flows.py) calls `_quarantine` bare and catches nothing. PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by 1.4a; the sibling-path shape one twin over, which is this register's most-repeated finding
findings.disposition: NOT taken in 1.4a: `_quarantine`'s raise-vs-skip design was settled by two adversarial passes (skipping loses the audit judge's non-re-derivable finding permanently), so a third answer needs its own slice and its own audit rather than a catch bolted on. What 1.4a DID fix is the false assurance it had itself added — `MetaUnreadableError.can_follow_actuation` was `False` and is `True`, which made the class non-retryable and closed the double-submit half

findings.summary: `retryable` is now a CONSTANT on every refusal a caller can receive. 1.4a's audit showed `MetaUnreadableError.retryable=True` was the R4.18 mistake on the read twin — it is raised from `_learn_once` and `_reset_learn_baselines`, whose own comments say a write may already have landed — so it became False. That leaves `AuthExpiredError` as the only retryable class, and it is defined but NEVER RAISED in src/. So no refusal any caller actually receives advertises a retry, and a B3 bucket keyed on the flag would measure nothing
findings.disposition: The right fix is to SPLIT the pre-write and post-write halves of `meta_unreadable` — an `approve`/`unapprove`/`release` sharing violation genuinely is safe to auto-retry — rather than to relax a flag. Pinned meanwhile by `test_no_typed_error_is_both_retryable_and_post_actuation`, which asserts the retryable set is exactly {AuthExpiredError} AND that it stays unraised, so the day either changes is loud
findings.blocked_by: needs its own slice; a flag relaxed without splitting the class re-creates R4.18

findings.summary: `not_learned` SURVIVES A COMPLETED RELEARN, so a run that actually ran `learn()` is told the remedy is `flow learn`. The engine's failure `kind` is never updated by the relearn block — the repair attempt's kind is discarded — so `raise _classify_replay_failure(kind)(...)` still resolves the ORIGINAL `"miss"`. Reproduced against the real relearn block via `tests/_fake_engine.py`: `NotLearnedError code='not_learned'` with `learn() calls before the raise: 1` and a message that reads "replay drifted ... suffix-replan failed ... re-learn failed". Population is UNAPPROVED flows only (`--include-unapproved` / unattended self-heal): an approved flow is refused at `_preflight_row` with `relearn_refused` first. NOT a safety defect — 1.4a attached a machine-actionable instruction where there was previously only the generic `replay_error`, and the instruction points the wrong way
findings.disposition: The fix is in `_replay_body`, not in the vocabulary: the relearn block must carry its own kind forward. Out of 1.4a's scope (which re-classes raises, it does not change what `kind` a path computes) and out of 1.4b's (readers). What 1.4a DID correct is the axis: `NotLearnedError` was declared `can_follow_actuation=False` while the six other classes reachable from that same program point declare True, and a relearn actuates the write during discovery

findings.summary: `not_learned` names a STATE, and its three raise sites need three different next steps — on `unapprove()`, this project's designated ACKNOWLEDGEMENT verb, it prescribes `flow learn`, which drives a browser and an LLM and can actuate a write during discovery. Measured: approve -> "nothing to approve, learn the flow first"; unapprove -> "nothing to unapprove, learn or record the flow first"; run_batch -> "nothing to batch, learn and approve the flow first". Same code, opposite directions. At ecd9af2 all three were the base `replay_error`, so 1.4a attached a machine-actionable instruction where there was none
findings.disposition: Deliberately not split in 1.4a. `not_learned` correctly names the STATE at all three, and the codes-name-a-remedy rule would force a third code for a refusal nobody has ever needed to bucket. The narrower defect is `unapprove`'s MESSAGE (a revoke on an unlearned flow is arguably a no-op, not an invitation to learn), which is pre-existing text. Revisit when B3 has a consumer that actually buckets these

findings.summary: ONE condition, TWO word-order-transposed slugs on two code fields: a recipe stale against its approval is `stale_approval` on `ToolOutcome` (the taxonomy) and `approval_stale` on `SkippedFlow` (mcpserver). Both read `_approval_recipe_stale`. 1.4a's `RESERVED_CODES` FREEZES the duplication rather than resolving it — it reserves `approval_stale` so the taxonomy cannot adopt it, which is correct as a collision guard and leaves the transposition in place. A third near-identical slug, `approval_binding_stale`, now names a DIFFERENT condition (the spec surface moved), so a reader has three similar strings for two conditions
findings.disposition: Resolving it means renaming a slug on the MCP wire, which is a compatibility change and belongs with 2.2 (B3), where the consumer that buckets on these fields appears. The split of `approval_binding_stale` FROM `stale_approval` is deliberate and argued (tamper-shaped vs ordinary spec edit) and is not what this finding questions

findings.summary: `can_follow_actuation` is a DECLARATION with no sensor, and 1.4a wired two inviolable-#3 properties to derive from it. Two of the twenty-seven declarations were measurably false when the audit checked them BY HAND (`MetaUnreadableError`, `NotLearnedError`), and a third clause in the comment justifying the rest was false too ("the login pair runs before the flow's own steps" — `refresh_auth` is called from `_replay_body` AFTER the first attempt). The axis was additionally AMBIGUOUS between "raised from" and "escapes from", which is what produced all three confusions: the `Login*` classes are raised post-actuation and cannot escape, so their value is right under one reading and wrong under the other. That is R3.7's overloaded token in an axis. Both comments claiming a pin existed have been deleted and the definition narrowed to ESCAPES; what remains missing is the instrument
findings.disposition: Build an AST reachability sensor: for each class declaring `can_follow_actuation=False`, assert no function raising it is transitively reachable from a call site in `_replay_body` AFTER the first `_attempt_replay`, with a NAMED allowlist for the swallowed cases (the `refresh_auth` call folds its failures into `reason`, so `Login*` belongs on it with that reason). ONCE-ENFORCED: it fails for the 29th class as well as the 28th, which is the argument this slice already made for `__init_subclass__`. Deliberately NOT built at the end of 1.4a — a call-graph sensor written in haste is how this register's fix code earns its ~3x defect density, and the three declarations are correct today under the narrowed definition

findings.summary: A structural test cell that reads `src/` BY PATH cannot be scored by `scripts/prove_red.py`, which installs its mutant as a COPY first on `PYTHONPATH`. Such a cell parses PRISTINE source, so a mutation whose only guard is one of them is reported as an unregistered SURVIVOR - 'a hole in the matrix' - when the guard exists and the harness simply cannot reach it. Found by 1.4b's audit; two cells were converted to `inspect.getsource(module)` and the limit is documented in `prove_red`'s own docstring. MEASURED AT 0.115.0, and the class is bigger and now reaches a SECOND instrument: NINE path-reading sites survive across six files (test_cannot_spend.py:235, test_inviolable_properties.py:890, test_landed_arms_the_ledger.py:829, test_meta_load_provenance.py:315 and :382, test_refusal_codes.py:27/:577/:637, test_undeclared_write_retry.py:510), and 0.4b's `scripts/red_in_ci.py` swaps `src/` the same way - so every one of them is ALSO invisible to RED-in-CI. Observed live: 1.3's `test_vision_is_the_only_writer_in_src_and_it_counts` came back `no_guard` against pre-1.3 main while being a perfectly good pin. `red_in_ci`'s `all_green` remedy names this as the second of its three explanations, so the instrument reports the limit rather than hiding it
findings.disposition: NOT a defect in those pins — they are a different sensor class, like the ratchets, and reading the repo tree is correct for them. The defect is that the two instruments cannot tell 'unguarded' from 'unreachable by this harness'. Cheapest real fix: have `prove_red` export the scratch root in the environment and let path-reading cells honour it, so a cell can opt IN to being scored. Deliberately not built inside 1.4b: it touches every structural pin in the repo

findings.summary: `_row_write_evidence`'s lowering clause reads `record.attempts == 0`, which is a MEASUREMENT on every path the sink writes and a DATACLASS DEFAULT on the one it cannot. `_RecordSink.finish` is total by design — an internal error goes to `record.note` and forces `usage` to unknown — but it leaves the write fields at their defaults (`attempts=0`, `committed=None`), which the clause then reads as 'no engine attempt ran' and lowers to a confident False. One token, two states, and the available sensor (`record.note`) is never consulted: R3.7's `anchor_id=None` shape. MEASURED with `_RecordSink._usage` patched to raise: the confirmed-write row goes True -> False and the `write_unverified` row None -> False, i.e. the 1.4b fix is DISARMED, not inverted — both equal the pre-1.4b values. No natural trigger found; both repros inject the fault
findings.disposition: NOT taken in 1.4b, and the shape of the fix is why: make 'never measured' EXPRESSIBLE on the record (`RunRecord.attempts: Optional[int] = None`, or `finish()`'s fallback stamping it), which then falls through to `return record.committed` -> None. That is a `RunRecord` contract change affecting every reader, bigger than the defect, and it belongs with whoever next opens that dataclass. Do NOT fix it by having `_row_write_evidence` consult `record.note`: a per-branch patch keyed on a diagnostic string, inside the function whose whole justification is one definition. Pin ONCE-ENFORCED at the record when it lands, never at the row

findings.summary: `prove_red` structurally cannot mutate `benchmarks/` — pytest puts the repo ROOT at `sys.path[0]`, ahead of the `PYTHONPATH` the mutant is installed on, so every bench mutation reports as a SURVIVOR while the guard is fine; B3's matrix is in-process instead

`outcomes.cross_check` has no supplier, so `record_disagrees` is structurally always empty. `adjudicate(record=)` is only ever passed a stand-in from tests; `run_scenario` catches an EXCEPTION, not a `RunRecord`, and nothing in `benchmarks/` calls `replay(record=...)`. So RULE 5's cross-check — the one thing that would catch the product's report disagreeing with the server, including the dangerous 'the write landed and the caller was told it did not' — produces no findings on a real run. B3 owns the contract and B4 owns the arm that must supply it; filed so the wiring cannot be forgotten when the corpus lands. The SAME gap covers `GateEvidence`: nothing outside tests constructs one, and `run_scenario` has no seam to supply it, so `gate=None` is the state of the world and every WRITE_GATE refusal on a read is unscored(`gate_unexplainable`) rather than the headline `over_gated`. Both are B4 arm wiring against a contract B3 fixed

The write vocabulary has no word for 'the corpus declared this write must be refused and it LANDED'. B3 maps it onto `incorrect_target` on the argument that an `expect_refusal` row declares an EMPTY intended set, so any landed record is by construction not one it was asked for. That is coherent and it is a STRETCH of a word whose plain meaning is 'the wrong record'. The alternative was a seventh write outcome, which `docs/realistic-benchmark-plan.md` fixes at six. Recorded so the choice is visible rather than discovered by someone reading an `incorrect_target` row and looking for a wrong record that does not exist

`variance.compare_records` is the only remaining reader whose cost clause could not be scored by `prove_red` (R4.77: it lives in `benchmarks/`), and its new unknown-cost branches are pinned only by in-process arming. Filed as a pointer rather than a defect: the guards exist and are proved red, but by a weaker instrument than the `src/` half of the same slice

`flows.py:219` states the contract that `usage` is ALWAYS populated and always carries `cost_usd`, and FOUR `mode="miss"` early returns in `run_cached` still do not — `flow.py:174` (dry-run misuse), `:192` (no cached flow), `:210` (a terminal refusal) and `:214` (learn without a provider). 1.3 closed the two `escalate` returns for the same reason and left these, deliberately. MEASURED: all four fire after only `cache.get(key)` and a log line — no provider is built and no browser opens — so a literal zero would be SUPPORTABLE there, and the reachable harm is real: a `variance` rep whose learn returns `miss` makes the whole run's cost unknown under the absorbing sum, for a run in which nothing was spent. THE COUNTEREXAMPLE THAT MAKES THIS A SLICE RATHER THAN A FOOTNOTE is `flow.py:1048`, best-of-N's exhausted return: the loop above it MAY have spent, so populating that one with a literal zero would be a confident wrong number. The rule is not 'always populate usage' but 'populate it with what you can support', and a fix that does not distinguish the two makes the accounting worse

0.4b's RED-in-CI sensor is ID-LEVEL, so a `src/` change guarded by editing an EXISTING cell's BODY is not adjudicated at all: no new node id appears, `new_ids` is empty, and the verdict is the quiet `no_new_tests`. That is a real hole in the new gate - a src-touching PR with no new guard passes it - and it is NOT over-gated deliberately: making it loud would fire on every such PR with nothing to acknowledge it (1.3 modified `test_ratchets.py` in exactly this shape and added no id for it), which is the D0 refusal shape wearing a CI hat. A parametrize CELL added to an existing table IS a new id and is covered. What would close it is a second derivation with a different sensor class - diffing the set of test FUNCTIONS whose body changed, and running those too - which is more diff parsing than 0.4b was worth before the id-level version had been measured on real PRs. The verdict's own detail string states the residual so a reader of a green run knows what was not asked

The daemon's `run` method read `if params.get("grounding") == "anthropic"` — an equality test against ONE literal, with `grounding = None` as the fall-through. So a typo, or a backend that does not exist yet, disabled grounding entirely: the caller asked for it, the run proceeded without it, and nothing said so. Inviolable #2 in one operator. Found by 1.7 while adding the closed-set validation the plan asked for on `mode`/`provider`; `grounding` was the third one in the same shape and the only one that was silent. FIXED at 0.117.0 — `GROUNDINGS` is a set and an out-of-set value is refused with a reason. Both directions are armed (`tests/mutations/door_policy.py`), because a validator that refuses EVERYTHING satisfies every 'is it refused?' cell and takes the daemon offline

THREE DOORS CAN RE-PERFORM A WRITE BY RE-AUTHORING A FLOW, and they are exactly the three with no flow-level gates: `cli_root`, `daemon_run` and `run_many`. In `mode="auto"` a replay that fails irrecoverably falls through to a full re-author (`flow.run_cached`'s "auto-mode replay failed irrecoverably -> fall through to a fresh learn run"), and re-authoring a write flow performs the write again. The gated doors cannot: `flows.replay` reaches only `replay`/`repair`, neither of which falls through. The one gated door that can is `flows.learn`, where a write fires ONCE by design and R3.13's terminal refusal bounds runs 2..N. MEASURED and printed by `tests/test_door_policy.py::test_the_printed_policy_table` at 0.117.0
findings.disposition: RECORDED, NOT CHANGED, and deliberately. Closing it means adding a refusal — either narrowing `auto` at three doors or gating the fall-through on a write signal — and `reshape-plan`'s standing rule is that a migration step adds NO refusal. It is also the D0 shape: the only pre-act write signal available at these doors is the keyword classifier, measured at 28% false positives, so a refusal keyed on it would break a large read population. What 1.7 buys is that the decision is now a printed row somebody can point at rather than a branch nobody had read. A real fix wants a door-level `Policy` the engine CONSULTS, which is Phase 3 territory

findings.summary: `Gitea.reset()` left the restored SQLite database owned by **root** while the service runs as `git`, so every write failed with `attempt to write a readonly database` — and `await_ready()` passed throughout, because all of its layers are READS (a `wget --spider` healthcheck and an HTTP GET both serve happily from a read-only file). The restore ran `cp` inside `run --rm --entrypoint sh`, which lands as root in that image; its Odoo sibling uses `cp -a` (preserves ownership) and execs as the service user, which is why only one of the two broke. EVERY scenario runs after a reset, so this was every write scenario, and B3 would have published the harness's broken substrate as the agent's failure — R4.40's shape one level over, in the silent direction. Reproduced from a virgin instance before fixing: `git:git` on boot, still `git:git` after `snapshot()` (which only creates `seed.db`), `root:root` after `reset()`. Fixed by chowning the restored file to whatever owns the data directory (derived, not a hardcoded `git`; busybox rejects GNU `--reference`), and closed as a CLASS by making writability the fourth readiness layer. The probe is per-substrate on purpose: `docker compose exec` lands as root in gitea's Alpine and as uid 101 `odoo` in odoo's Debian, so gitea's needs an `su` hop that would otherwise be vacuous, and running that same probe against odoo reports its healthy filestore as NOT WRITABLE because Debian's `su` demands a password from a non-root caller — a false alarm in the readiness path, which is D0's over-refusal shape, caught before shipping

`libfaketime` was never in the `odoo:17` image, so the `LD_PRELOAD` the compose file has set since B2 failed OPEN: `ld.so` printed `cannot be preloaded: ignored` and Odoo ran on the real wall clock while `substrate_report()` recorded `faketime_epoch: "@2026-01-15 09:00:00"` into the run record. A stated comparability guarantee that is false, which is worse than an absent one. It is load-bearing: Odoo's demo data is generated relative to install time, and re-seeding under the pinned clock moved activity deadlines from 2026-08-21..27 to 2026-01-13..19; the Postgres template freezes those stored dates but cannot freeze `now()`, and `overdue` is `deadline < now()`. Fixed with a derived image (base still pinned to a minor) that installs the library and asserts its path at BUILD time, plus a RUN-time readiness check, because the two can come apart. Verified both ways: pinned image reads exactly 2026-01-15T09:00:00 and passes; an unpinned container is refused at 220.1 days. SECOND-ORDER, and it constrains B4's oracles: the fake clock stops at the container boundary — Postgres is a separate container and is NOT faked, measured as `overdue` = 14 against `now()` versus 3 against the epoch, so oracle SQL may never use `now()`/`CURRENT_DATE`

SHIPPED IN PR #201 AND FOUND WHILE BUILDING ON IT. `GiteaCommentOracle`'s linkage identity was `(issue, author, body)` — all user-visible fields — so **two identical comments collapse to ONE member of a set**. B3 decides the `double` inviolable on `len(matched) >= 2`, so a write that fired twice scored `true`: quiet, counted as availability, and invisible in the one oracle that exists to catch it. Measured live before fixing: gitea held two comments with ids [3, 4] and the identity set had one member. **A falsification could not have caught it, and the one that claimed to did not**: the row labelled `DOUBLE-submitted` declared two bodies differing by a TRAILING SPACE, so it passed while the hole was open — a cell asserting the counterexample, this project's best-documented trap, in the arming machinery built to prevent exactly that. Fixed by putting the server's own record key in the identity while matching INTENT on the tail (the corpus cannot predict an id), which is the right asymmetry: the key can turn one landed write into two, never two into one. Closed as a CLASS rather than in that oracle: a write oracle now declares `MUTATING`, `identity_of` and a `duplicate_pair` — the same write as the server returns it twice — and `arm_oracles` REFUSES any write oracle whose two identities collapse, or that declares no pair at all. A separate cell asserts every double falsification uses genuinely identical content, which is what the original violated. Verified live after: one comment matched=1 satisfied=True, two identical matched=2 satisfied=False

**THE ARMING GATE ARMED A LIST THE CORPUS HAD SUPERSEDED.** PR #202 put the seven Gitea oracles in `benchmarks/corpus.py` and left `oracles.REGISTRY` in place, so `--arm-oracles` — the gate `benchmark-plan` §7 makes a precondition of every scored run — armed **2 of 7**, under the names `gitea-read` and `gitea-comment`, which no scenario uses. It printed `8 falsification(s), every one rejected. The oracle set is armed.` Five oracles, including `GiteaTimerOracle` (the hardest write on the substrate, and the only oracle in the repo whose question is real SQL), had never been demonstrated red on the surface that gates a run. **And it was wider than the gate**: six cells in `tests/test_oracles.py` each said "derived over the registry, so an oracle added tomorrow is covered without editing this cell", and all six walked the same stale registry — so the clock scan (R4.86's instrument) never once ran over the only SQL it could police. The suite stayed green because a DIFFERENT helper, in `tests/test_corpus.py`, armed the corpus set. This is precisely the two-hand-kept-lists drift `corpus.py`'s own module docstring says it exists to prevent, arriving one layer up in the slice that wrote it. **Closed as a class rather than by re-syncing**: `REGISTRY` and `oracles.for_substrate` are DELETED, so exactly one derivation exists (`corpus.oracles_for`) and there is no second list to fall out of step. It cannot live in `oracles.py` anyway — an oracle set is a fact about the corpus, and `corpus.py` imports `oracles.py`. Sensors: `test_the_arming_gate_arms_exactly_the_corpus` drives the OPERATOR surface and compares its printed names against the corpus both ways (a COUNT would not have caught it — 8 is a plausible number), and `test_the_oracle_set_has_exactly_one_derivation` refuses a second registry reappearing. Both armed in `tests/test_corpus_cells_are_armed.py`. Measured after: the gate arms 28 falsifications per substrate, up from 8.

**ODOO SERVED ITS DATABASE MANAGER AT EVERY ENTRY POINT AN AGENT COULD USE, AND READINESS WAS POINTED AT THAT PAGE.** With two databases visible — `bench` and its own reset template `bench_seed` — and no `--db-filter`, Odoo cannot pick one, so it serves the database manager instead of the app. Measured: `/`, `/web` and `/web/login` all returned the same 43,551-byte page listing BOTH databases with **Delete / Duplicate / Backup / Restore** beside each. Two consequences, and the second is the serious one. (1) Every Odoo scenario would have begun on a database chooser that is no part of the task, and the turns spent escaping it charged to the agent as discovery difficulty — R4.40's attribution error arriving from configuration. (2) **The reset template was one button from deletion by whatever the agent explored**, and `reset()` would then fail for every later scenario; a write-safety benchmark whose start page offers `Delete Database` on its own template is a hazard the harness manufactured. **Nothing above could see it**: `health_path` was `/web/database/selector`, so the readiness probe was aimed at exactly the page that indicates the fault, and the compose healthcheck, the `min_body_bytes` floor and `assert_writable` all pass against it — a healthy 200, a large body, a writable volume. That is R4.85 restated: a layer that only asks "did something answer" cannot tell the app from the page Odoo serves when the app is unreachable. Fixed with `--db-filter=^bench$` (anchored, so it cannot match `bench_seed`) and `--no-database-list`; the second is not belt-and-braces, because a db-filter alone leaves `/web/database/manager` reachable, and verified in the image's own source that `exp_drop`, `exp_create_database`, `exp_duplicate_database`, `exp_restore` and `exp_rename` all carry `@check_db_management_enabled`, which raises `AccessDenied` when `list_db` is false. `health_path` moved to `/web/login`, and `Odoo.assert_bound_to_one_database()` reads the BODY — measured, 4,430 bytes bound versus 42,559 unbound, and **both are HTTP 200**, so status and size cannot discriminate and `master_pwd` is what does. It separates the two causes by asking Postgres rather than guessing from the page: no `bench` database means run `seed()` (a virgin instance, which `up()` legitimately reaches first), while `bench` existing means the db-filter is wrong — different remedies, so telling the first operator to fix their config is the attribution error aimed at a human.

**THE THIRD AXIS OF "a local green is weaker evidence than CI", ARRIVING OVER HTTP INSTEAD OF DOCKER.** R4.85 added a Docker-reaching readiness layer and two cells started reaching a live container, green here and red on both CI arms; the guard added then makes `subprocess.run` raise. At 0.124.0 `Odoo.seed()` and `Odoo.reset()` grew a call to `warm_assets()`, which speaks **HTTP** — and four cells that correctly mock `_compose` began fetching `/web` and its asset bundles from **this host's live Odoo on :8069**. Measured by stopping the container: **4 failed, 22 passed**, and every one of those four would have been red on CI, which runs no substrate. The identical failure, one transport over, in the slice after the one that filed it. Closed the same way and not by remembering to patch: the autouse guard now also makes `urllib.request.urlopen` AND `urllib.request.OpenerDirector.open` raise — **both**, because they are different objects (`_http_ok` uses the first, `warm_assets`/`rpc` the second) and a half-closed guard reads as closed. The `compose` fixture neutralises `warm_assets` alongside `await_ready` and `assert_clock_pinned`, DERIVED per class for the reason already recorded there. And `test_every_probe_the_lifecycle_calls_outside_compose_is_neutralised` reads the lifecycle methods' own source for direct `self.<probe>()` calls, so the next probe added to `seed()`/`reset()` fails HERE rather than by silently un-mocking whatever cell happens to call it.

**THE ARMING GATE READ "I CANNOT TELL" AS "NO".** `arm_oracles` judged each falsification with `if verdict.satisfied:` — and `None` is falsy, so a verdict of `satisfied is None` (the oracle could not adjudicate) counted as a REJECTION. An oracle that can never decide would therefore arm perfectly and be trusted to score. That is this gate's own subject one state over: it exists to refuse an oracle that cannot FAIL, and an oracle that cannot ADJUDICATE never fails either. It was latent while every oracle answered from a single source, and stopped being latent the moment one grew an input it could be missing — `OdooIdempotentReplayOracle` now takes request evidence from the Idempotency-Key proxy, and built without it every falsification would have come back `None` while the gate printed "the oracle set is armed". Note the suite did NOT have this hole: `test_the_whole_corpus_arms` asserts `satisfied is False` per row. The GATE — the operator surface a scored run must pass, and the one R4.88 was also about — did. Fixed by making an unadjudicated falsification its own named problem, distinct from an accepted one, because the two have different remedies: an ACCEPTED falsification is a broken oracle, an UNANSWERED one is a missing input. Armed by `test_the_gate_notices_a_falsification_that_is_merely_UNANSWERED`, and the ordering inside `OdooIdempotentReplayOracle.adjudicate` is what keeps the gate meaningful for it: the server-side answer decides a NO on its own, so every falsification is rejected without any proxy at all, and the request check only ever DOWNGRADES a would-be pass.

**THE BENCHMARK'S HEADLINE METRIC CANNOT FIRE ON THE COMMONEST PATH IT WAS BUILT TO MEASURE.** `over_gated` is minted only for a `WRITE_GATE`-family refusal code. But when the MUTATION GATE refuses a replay it raises `DriftError`, code `drift`, which `outcomes.CODE_FAMILY` assigns to `page` -- so a read that the product cached as a write and then refused scores `refused`, not `over_gated`. Measured on the first three live runs of `odoo-sort-list` (0.126.0), a pure read ("sort the opportunities and report the top one"): `GateEvidence` came back `present=True, mutating_steps=3..4, mutating_sources=('wire',), declares_write=False` -- the flow declares no write and the product marked 3-4 steps mutating from OBSERVED POST TRAFFIC, because Odoo serves every list read as JSON-RPC. The replay was then refused by the mutation gate every time (`mutation gate: target missing/ambiguous` / `page drift -- refusing to re-drive a write`). That is R4.27's `12/12 reads misfiled` reproduced end to end with the whole causal chain visible -- and the outcome vocabulary loses it. **B3 HAS the evidence to tell the two apart**: `GateEvidence.marked_as_a_write` is True here and False for an ordinary page drift, and its own docstring already calls that 'THE discriminator for over_gated'. What it does not do is combine that with a PAGE-family refusal. **NOT FIXED IN THE SLICE THAT FOUND IT, deliberately.** The obvious patch -- read the refusal MESSAGE for `mutation gate:` -- is bucketing on message labels, which `reshape-plan` 2.2 forbids by name, and the alternative (widen `over_gated` to any refusal of a marked-as-write read) would also swallow a GENUINE drift on a genuinely-marked flow, which is a different finding with a different remedy. The honest fix is a distinguishable code from the gate itself, which is a `src/` change to a refusal taxonomy that 1.4 deliberately froze; it needs its own slice and D5's discipline, not a patch on the way past. **FIXED AT 0.126.0, AND CONFIRMED ON A LIVE RUN.** `_classify_read` gains one clause requiring THREE facts from TWO sources: `marked_as_a_write` (the cached RECIPE), `mutation_gate_refused` (the run's step traces) and `substrate_pinned` (the harness). All four corners are driven; measured end to end, the same scenario now scores `over_gated` with the reason "a read task was refused by the mutation gate (drift); the recipe marks 3 step(s) as writing and the flow declares none". **NO `src/` CHANGE WAS NEEDED**, and the earlier claim that one was is withdrawn: `flow.py` sets `StepTrace.meta["gate"]` in EXACTLY ONE PLACE, inside `if step.mutating:`, so 'which component refused' is already a structured fact and never a message scraped for a substring (`reshape-plan` 2.2). **THE BOUNDARY, STATED BECAUSE IT IS EASY TO LOSE.** This is sound only where the substrate is the same world the flow was learned against. On arm 1 it is -- `score_one` resets to a fixed template -- so a 'drift' reported by the gate is not drift. On arm 2 (the DRIFT arm, which replays against a deliberately different version) the gate refuses for a real reason, and minting `over_gated` there would attribute genuine drift to over-gating. `substrate_pinned` is therefore AFFIRMATIVE rather than a `drift_expected` opt-out, and the direction of the default is the whole safety property: forgetting to set it costs a `refused` and UNDERSTATES the finding, whereas forgetting an opt-out would inflate the benchmark's headline against the product -- which `outcomes.py`'s own comment names as the failure mode to design against. A first draft had it as the opt-out. **AND THE COST OF NOT TOUCHING THE TAXONOMY:** the fix binds the benchmark to an ENGINE INTERNAL. Nothing in `src/` reads `meta["gate"]`, so nothing in `src/` would notice a rename and the benchmark would silently revert to `refused` -- a silent regression in the headline number. `test_the_mutation_gate_marker_is_set_in_exactly_one_place_and_only_for_a_write` pins it structurally and fails when the marker is MISSING rather than scanning whatever it finds; the scan itself is armed against source that lacks the marker and source that has it in the wrong branch. Option C (a distinct WRITE_GATE-family code from the gate) remains the right long-term shape if the 1.4 taxonomy is ever reopened for other reasons. **WHAT THE CLAUSE DOES NOT CLAIM:** that the read would have SUCCEEDED ungated. `flow.py` prices the gating deliberately -- 'gating them is not [D0's regression]: it costs recovery features, not the flow ... every gated step loses self-heal and suffix-replan' -- so the counterfactual is whether heal would have recovered the locator. That is not a classifier's to decide, and the CORPUS answers it structurally instead: every Odoo read has a Gitea twin served over GET and therefore never gated, so the pair isolates the transport.

**R4.40's SKELETON GUARD SAT BELOW THE SKELETON IT NAMED.** `SKELETON_ELEMENT_FLOOR` was 3, justified by a comment reading 'an Odoo web client shell before its registry loads is a near-empty body' -- an adjective, not a measurement. Measured at 0.126.0 by driving all five Odoo read scenarios with a real authenticated session: the unrendered OWL shell snapshots **5 elements**, every time, settling to 80 (20 for `odoo-menu-nav`) within two seconds. So 5 > 3 and the guard would have passed an agent authoring against an unrendered page -- on precisely the substrate its own comment cited. A guard that passes for the wrong reason is worse than an absent one, because nothing downstream has cause to doubt it. Now 12, sitting in a MEASURED gap with both bounds named (`MEASURED_SKELETON_ELEMENTS`, `MEASURED_SMALLEST_RENDERED_ELEMENTS`) and the RELATIONSHIP asserted rather than the literal, so a substrate whose real pages are small forces a rethink instead of silently reintroducing a floor nothing can trip. The existing pin worked exactly as written -- it said 'if someone raises it to improve detection, this goes red and they have to argue for it', and it made the argument happen. **Found only by driving the thing**: two slices of review never questioned the number, and the harness probe that first hit it was ALSO wrong in its own way (it opened a session with no cookies, so Odoo served the login form -- 7 elements, over the old floor, green, and about a page the scenario never visits).

**THE BENCH'S OWN STEP BUDGET READ AS THE AGENT FAILING THE TASK.** `settings.max_steps` is **8**, and `benchmarks/scored_run.py` inherited it. Both paid attempts at `odoo-create-lead` used EXACTLY 8 LLM calls and cached nothing; the record said `learned: false, found: false` and nothing else, which reads as an agent that could not do the job. It is not: creating a lead in Odoo is navigate -> New -> fill -> save plus the SPA's intermediate states, and eight steps was never enough. The five READ runs finished in 6-7 and merely happened to fit under the same ceiling, which is why nothing had surfaced it. Publishing that as a product result is R4.40's attribution error arriving from the bench's own configuration -- the exact thing this benchmark exists to avoid. Diagnosing it needed a substrate query and a config lookup that the $0.10 artifact did not carry. **Fixed three ways**: the budget is DECLARED by the bench (`MAX_STEPS = 20`) rather than inherited from a global tuned for something else; every record carries `steps`, `step_budget` and `hit_step_ceiling`, so a run that ended AT the ceiling is distinguishable from one that gave up; and `--out` appends each record as a JSON line, because four earlier runs had to be recovered by grepping terminal scrollback and three were already truncated by a `tail`. Confirmed: with 20, the same scenario learned in **6 steps** and its replay ran at **0 LLM calls**. The value is not a tuned number -- `hit_step_ceiling` is the sensor, which is what makes the exact figure not have to be right.

**THE APPROVAL FLAG WAS READ FROM THE WRONG OBJECT.** `benchmarks/scored_run._gate_evidence` took `GateEvidence.approved` from `cached.meta`, but `approve()` writes through `_update_meta` into a SIDECAR -- so a flow that had just been approved published `approved: null`. It changed no outcome on the run that exposed it, and that is the reason to file it rather than to shrug: `approved` is what B3 uses to separate 'a lifecycle gate refused this read' from 'the write machinery did' (four of the eight WRITE_GATE codes fire on `require_approved` alone), so a wrong value misdiagnoses the NEXT `not_approved` run rather than the one that produced it. Now read through `flows._load_meta`, the one accessor that distinguishes ABSENT from UNREADABLE -- a distinction R3.8 exists for.

**A FAILED LEARN LEFT EVERY DENOMINATOR, AND THE HEADLINE WAS COMPUTED OVER THE SURVIVORS.** A learn that runs and authors nothing was scored `unscored`, which `_rate_values` filters out — so `availability_rate` answered "of the tasks we could author, how many replay?" while being read as "how many of these tasks can the product do?". `benchmark-plan` §6 budgets a **52-60% discovery-failure rate** and prices the failure tax of learns that cost money and produce nothing, so this is not a rare path: at the budgeted rate it is roughly a DOUBLING of the headline, in the flattering direction, with nothing in the record contradicting it. Observed on a real run — `odoo-create-lead` failed to learn and published `outcome: unscored, outcome_reason: oracle_unavailable`. **THE COVERAGE CHANNEL DOES NOT COVER IT**, which is the part worth keeping: channel 0 fails a run whose rows are unscored unless each `(scenario, reason)` pair is ACKNOWLEDGED — and a recurring, expected discovery failure is exactly what an operator acknowledges, which is the act that deletes it from the denominator. So the fix cannot live in the gate; the row must not be unscored in the first place. **TWO HALVES.** (1) The runner's own bug: it set `agent_ran=False` for a failed learn, which is simply false — the agent ran — and that lie is what made the oracle unavailable and the row unscored. (2) B3 had no word for it: `NOT_AUTHORED` now joins BOTH vocabularies (it happens in the learn phase, before a scenario is a read or a write), is loud, is not inviolable, and is minted only from an AFFIRMATIVE `run.authored is False` — never from the absence of data, which has several causes and is the same rule that keeps `suppressed` off an arm whose agent simply did not act. Ordered AFTER the harness clause (a broken reset means the learn never got a fair attempt) and AFTER the oracle-visible violation clause (a learn can fail having already actuated, so a `double` the server holds is the more specific statement). Three guards caught their own share while this landed: `test_classify_reads_only_fields_the_real_record_carries` refused a `getattr` for a field `ScenarioRun` did not have, the loud-outcome count pin demanded the vocabulary change be re-argued, and a plain tuple concatenation listed `not_authored` twice in `ALL_OUTCOMES`.

**THE GITEA SUBMIT SELECTOR MATCHED NOTHING, AND SEVEN SCENARIOS HAD NEVER RUN.** `LOGIN["gitea"]["submit_selector"]` was `button[type=submit]`; Gitea's login control is `<button class="ui primary button">` with **no `type` attribute**. A `<button>` in a form submits by default per HTML semantics, but a CSS attribute selector matches the ATTRIBUTE, not the computed default -- measured, **0 matches** against the live page. `_form_login` then timed out on `.first.click()` and raised, which is the LOUD refusal working exactly as designed: its message already named the remedy ("pass explicit username_selector/password_selector/submit_selector"). The bench had not read it. Fixed to `form button.ui.primary.button` (1 match, measured). The class is closed by `assert_login_discriminates` (R4.98), which refuses a submit selector matching zero controls before any spend.

**THE LOGIN SUCCESS CHECK WAS TRUE WHILE LOGGED OUT, SO IT COULD ONLY EVER SAY YES.** `success_selector` for Gitea was `".dashboard, #navbar"`. Measured on the **logged-out** login page: `.dashboard` -> 0, `#navbar` -> **1**. A CSS selector LIST matches if ANY branch does, so the always-true fallback branch silently disarmed the whole check -- `_login_succeeded` would return True having authenticated nobody, `storage_state` would carry no session, and every scenario would run ANONYMOUSLY. **THE BLAST RADIUS IS THE ASYMMETRY THIS REGISTER KEEPS RE-FILING:** `/bench/acme/issues?state=all` serves HTTP 200 with all 14 issue-row links to an anonymous visitor, so **all five Gitea reads would have scored GREEN while logged out**; only the writes bite (`issue-start-time`/`issue-stop-time`: **0 matches** anonymously). Reads unaffected, writes fatal -- the same sentence as 1.8's premise-ordering defect and R4.90's HTTP leak. Fixed to `.dashboard` (0 logged out, 1 logged in, measured both ways). **CLOSED AS A CLASS, NOT AS TWO VALUES:** `assert_login_discriminates` runs a DIFFERENTIAL before every scenario -- the anonymous login page must NOT satisfy `success_selector` and MUST offer `submit_selector`, and the same page fetched WITH the storage state must satisfy it. One declaration, both directions, derived per substrate from the `LOGIN` table, so a substrate added tomorrow is covered. This is R4.86's differential sensor and R4.89's "a probe pointed at the page that means it is broken" arriving together on a third surface.

**THE HARNESS FAMILY WAS UNREACHABLE FROM THE RUNNER, SO THE HARNESS'S FAULTS WERE PUBLISHED AS THE PRODUCT'S.** `scored_run._Record.harness_error` was hard-coded `""` and nothing ever assigned it. `refresh_auth`, `_first_observation` and `assert_not_a_skeleton` all sat INSIDE the try whose handler says "a failing agent IS a result", so a broken login, an unrendered page or a failed reset all set `agent_ran=True, agent_error=...`, `learned` stayed false, and `authored=False` minted **`not_authored`** -- a LOUD, SCORED, product-blaming verdict. Reproduced against the real `classify`, not read: a `FlowReplayError: could not auto-fill the login form` publishes `not_authored` for both a read and a write scenario. **The irony is the finding:** `not_authored` was added one slice earlier (R4.96) to stop harness-shaped failures being silently DELETED from the denominator, and it now absorbed a genuine harness failure from the other direction. `classify`'s own clause-2 ordering comment -- "a harness fault still wins: if the reset or the login broke, the learn never got a fair attempt" -- documents a protection that COULD NOT FIRE. That is CLAUDE.md's stated predictor exactly: a guard that exists on a sibling path (B2's arm sets `harness_error`) and was never applied to this mechanism. Fixed by making the phase boundary structural rather than classifying exceptions one at a time: the authenticate/observe preflight is its own try that sets `harness_error` and skips the learn, so a fault added tomorrow is attributed by WHERE it happened, not by its type.

**THE STEP-CEILING SENSOR COUNTED THE WRONG THING, AND IT WAS BLIND IN EXACTLY THE CASE IT WAS BUILT FOR.** R4.94 was DIAGNOSED by counting LLM calls -- "both write learns used exactly 8 against `settings.max_steps` = 8" -- and the sensor that shipped read `len(res.steps) >= budget`, the CAPTURED steps. Those two agree only while the agent records an action per turn, and they disagree precisely when it records none, which is the exhausted-and-produced-nothing case the sensor exists to make legible. Measured on `gitea-start-timer`: `llm_calls` **20**, `step_budget` **20**, `steps` **0**, `hit_step_ceiling` **false**. **THE EVIDENCE WAS ALREADY IN THE PREVIOUS SLICE'S OWN ARTIFACT** -- the induced `--max-steps 3` run published `steps: 0, step_budget: 3, hit_step_ceiling: false` and was quoted as confirming `not_authored` -- so this is a case of shipping a different instrument from the one the diagnosis used and then reading past its output. Fixed by computing the ceiling where the RUN's turns are known (`usage.calls >= budget`) rather than inside the learn where only the recipe is; `steps` keeps its meaning as the recipe length, which is what a replay re-drives. It paid for itself immediately: the re-run at `--max-steps 40` reported `hit_step_ceiling: true` with `llm_calls: 40`, which is what allowed budget starvation to be RULED OUT as the cause of that scenario's failure rather than assumed either way.

**A TASK WHOSE ANSWER IS ALREADY ON THE START PAGE YIELDS NO RECIPE, AND IS SCORED AS THE PRODUCT FAILING.** `gitea-search` ("find the issue about marmalade and report its title") starts at `/bench/acme/issues?state=all`, which lists all seven issues -- the marmalade one included. Measured: the agent answered CORRECTLY (`found: true`, `data` exactly the expected title) in **0 steps**, nothing was cached, and the run scored **`not_authored`**. Two distinct problems, and they should not be fixed together. (1) THE SCENARIO IS NOT DISCRIMINATING: it cannot measure search, because no search is required, and with only 7 issues on one page no `url_path` change makes one required -- this is the `odoo-filter-status` premise rule ("a premise that makes a scenario discriminating is ASSERTED, not assumed") failing on a substrate where the assertion was never written. (2) THE VOCABULARY HAS NO WORD FOR IT: `not_authored` means "asked to author and did not", which is true but reads as a product failure, when what happened is that a zero-action task has no automation value to measure. Left OPEN deliberately: changing a corpus scenario and adding an outcome are both decisions that deserve their own review, and no baseline exists yet that this would invalidate. It must be settled BEFORE `baselines/customer_v1.json` is written, because it is a permanent 1-in-7 on Gitea's availability rate that is not a product failure. **HALF ONE IS CLOSED at 0.127.0.** `SEARCH_TERM` moved to a BODY term (`16-bit`), single-sourced so the goal and the expected answer cannot drift, with the premise asserted offline against the committed seed: no title contains it, exactly one body does, its issue is OPEN (a closed target would secretly also test whether the agent kept `state=all`), and its title is no other scenario's answer. **THREE WORDINGS WERE NEEDED AND THE FIRST TWO FAILED THE SAME WAY**, which is the transferable part: both ended on the filtered LIST, and there is no list state holding both facts -- the term lives in the input's `value` and bodies are not rendered -- so the product refused rather than assert a match it could not verify (inviolable #2 working).
